title: The threads library: a blocking queue with Mutex and Condition
body: The `threads.posix` library gives OCaml system threads. `Thread.create f x` starts a thread, `Thread.join` waits for it, and `Thread.delay` sleeps. In OCaml 5 threads run inside a domain and share one runtime lock, so they interleave rather than run in parallel; they are the tool for overlapping *waiting* (input, timers, locks), while domains are the tool for parallel computation.

Shared state needs a `Mutex`. `Mutex.protect m f` locks, runs `f`, and always unlocks. To *wait* for a condition, such as 'the queue is not empty', use a `Condition`: `Condition.wait c m` atomically releases the mutex and sleeps, and re-acquires the mutex when another thread calls `Condition.signal c`. Always wait in a `while` loop that rechecks the condition, because a thread can wake when the condition is no longer true.

A bounded blocking queue uses two conditions, `not_empty` for consumers and `not_full` for producers. `pop` waits while the queue is empty, takes an item and signals `not_full`; `push` waits while the queue is at capacity, adds an item and signals `not_empty`. The tests start a consumer on an empty queue and a producer on a full one and check that each really blocks, which is the property a plain `Queue` does not have.
challenge: In src/bq.ml, `pop` raises on an empty queue and `push` ignores the capacity. Make both block: guard the queue with a mutex, add `not_empty` and `not_full` conditions, wait in `while` loops, and signal after every change.
projectInstructions: Run `dune test --root .`. Edit only src/bq.ml. A hang usually means a missing `Condition.signal`; a lost item means a missing `Mutex`.
question: Why wait on a Condition inside a `while` loop and not an `if`?
correct: A thread can wake up when the condition is no longer true, so it must recheck before proceeding
wrong: A while loop makes the wait shorter
Condition.wait returns immediately unless it is in a loop
reasoning: Another thread may have consumed the item between the signal and the wakeup, so the predicate has to be tested again after every wake.
